title: Subthalamic Nucleus and Globus Pallidus Neurons
intro: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) and the external globus pallidus (GPe) are two small basal ganglia nuclei wired into a loop: excitatory STN cells drive inhibitory GPe cells, which inhibit the STN back. Both are made of autonomous pacemakers, and the loop between them can either stay quiet and irregular or lock into oscillations. In Parkinson's disease it locks into exaggerated beta rhythms, which is why the STN is the most common target for deep brain stimulation.

items: STN neurons: glutamatergic, the only excitatory nucleus inside the basal ganglia. In rat there are only about 14,000 per side (Oorschot 1996), far fewer than the millions of striatal cells. They fire spontaneously at about 10 to 30 Hz in slices without any synaptic input, driven by persistent sodium and other subthreshold currents (Bevan & Wilson 1999).

Rebound bursts: hyperpolarisation of STN cells, for example by synchronous GPe inhibition, de-inactivates T-type calcium channels, so the end of inhibition triggers a rebound burst. This is the cellular basis of the STN-GPe oscillation.

GPe neurons: GABAergic, fast-firing pacemakers (often 30 to 80 Hz in vivo in primates, with occasional pauses; DeLong 1971) that keep firing in slices. Mallet et al. (2012) split them into prototypic cells (most of them, PV-positive, projecting to STN and the output nuclei) and arkypallidal cells (FoxP2-positive, projecting back to the striatum, where they may act as a stop signal).

Connections: STN receives the hyperdirect pathway straight from cortex (Nambu et al. 2002) and inhibition from GPe; it excites GPe and the output nuclei (GPi and SNr). GPe receives the striatal indirect pathway (D2 MSNs) and STN input.

Function: the hyperdirect pathway lets cortex quickly raise STN activity and broadly suppress actions, a global brake used when stopping or when choices conflict (Frank 2006). In decision models the STN normalises evidence across all competing actions.

Oscillations: Plenz and Kitai (1999) showed that co-cultured STN and GPe form a pacemaker that oscillates on its own. After dopamine loss, STN and GPe activity becomes synchronised in the beta band (about 13 to 30 Hz), and the strength of this beta correlates with motor slowing (Brown et al. 2001). High-frequency stimulation of the STN (around 130 Hz) relieves symptoms.

Terman, Rubin, Yew and Wilson (2002): small conductance-based STN and GPe neurons with T-type currents, wired in different patterns. Depending on connectivity and striatal input to GPe, the network shows irregular firing, clustered rhythms or travelling waves, mapping onto healthy and parkinsonian states.

Rubin and Terman (2004): added the thalamus and showed in the same framework how high-frequency STN stimulation can restore faithful thalamic relay by replacing a pathological rhythm with regular, high-rate output.

Holgado, Terry and Bogacz (2010): a two-population firing-rate model with delays that gives analytical conditions for beta oscillations in the STN-GPe loop; strong coupling (as after dopamine loss) pushes the loop over a Hopf bifurcation.
Detailed single-cell models: Otsuka et al. (2004) and Gillies and Willshaw (2006) built conductance-based STN models reproducing spontaneous firing, plateau potentials and rebound bursts.

Normative models: Bogacz and Gurney (2007) showed that the cortex-striatum-STN-GPe circuit can implement an asymptotically optimal statistical test between alternative actions, with the STN providing the normalisation term.

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: A loop of an excitatory and an inhibitory pacemaker population with rebound bursting is a ready-made oscillator. Its frequency is set by synaptic delays and time constants, and coupling strength decides whether it oscillates.
If you build basal-ganglia action selection into an agent, include a global, fast excitatory brake (the hyperdirect pathway via STN) as well as action-specific direct and indirect pathways.
Pathological synchrony is a warning for any recurrent E-I network you build: too-strong coupling between populations of pacemakers locks them into a rhythm that carries no information.
